doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Rock and pop projects: Kiss, Chicago, Japanese orchestral rock
summary: Berg worked with Kiss, Richard Marx, Elliott Smith and Japanese stars, adding orchestras to finished tracks, including a Schoenberg-style string version that hit number one in Japan.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yeah, it’s a gig. Drop some names on me. What are some of the rock bands, let’s see you did Chicago.
Well I’m so pleased that I got a Grammy nomination for working with Kiss.

Played piano and orchestrated for Kiss on their recent “Psycho Circus” album. And Gene Simmons actually is an interesting guy and when we were working with him I had a writing partner and we asked him how are the rehearsals going for the tour? He said, “What does it matter?” He said, “We can suck and fifty thousand people will come to every concert.” He said, “The problem with you jazz musicians is you want to play good for seventy-five dollars.”

I worked with Richard Marks on a couple of albums, who is a great pop star. I worked on an album for a guy named Elliot Smith that Billboard magazine named the number two album of the year last year, it was a really great alternative songwriter. So you never know. I mean I’ve worked with Mickey Gilley in country music and I’ve kind of worked with a wide variety, there’s some Japanese, I do a lot of work for Japanese superstars and they’ve got a whole sound. And I love that because this one guy I work with typically uses 80 or 90 piece orchestras on Japanese rock tunes. So it’s like doing a film score.
Do you usually get the assignment musically after the fact, after they’ve laid down most of the tune and then, okay, now what can you do with this?

Right. Typically that’s true. Depending. I mean obviously if you’re doing a scoring thing then you’re wide open but when you’re working with rock bands typically they’ve laid down tracks and then it’s your job to come in. So it’s an interesting kind of a straight jacket and yet you’re still trying to create something. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
I would guess, and sometimes it must be a challenge to — how can anything be put over this? That would be my sense.
Especially when it’s heavy metal and then there’s a ninety piece orchestra.
Yeah. There’s so much going on. Well. It’s a challenge.

It’s another one of those challenges and one time this Japanese guy that I work with had a kind of a power metal ballad thing. And he said I’d like to do an alternate version with just the lead vocal and fifty strings, and write whatever you want. And so now all I had was a lead vocal and I wasn’t married to the chord progression. And there was even about a twelve or sixteen bar guitar solo in the middle where now there was nothing. And I wrote like for Verkärte Nacht, Schoenberg, for those sixteen bars. And the guy loved it, and he released that instead of the original version, with totally different harmonies, and it went to number one in Japan. So that was about the one time I ever got a clean plate.
